title: Tail Risk Spillovers in Commodity Markets: A Copula-Based Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall Approach
affiliations: Agricultural University of Athens, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of East Anglia (UEA) - School of Economic and Social Studies

detail.title: Tail Risk Spillovers in Commodity Markets: A Copula-Based Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall Approach

keywords: Crude oil and Agricultural commodity futures

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the evolving dependence structure and tail risk spillovers between crude oil and major agricultural futures (wheat, corn, and soybeans) from January 2005 to December 2023. Using a GJR-GARCH model to estimate the marginal distributions and several dynamic copulas (Student-t, Gumbel, and Rotated Gumbel) within a Generalized Autoregressive Score (GAS) framework, we examine the time-varying co-movements and asymmetries across different crisis periods, including the global financial crisis, the European debt crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Russia–Ukraine war.We compute dynamic Value-at-Risk (VaR), Expected Shortfall (ES), and hedge ratios to assess the magnitude and direction of tail risk transmission, with a special focus on lower-tail dependence. The results reveal stronger downside risk spillovers from oil to agricultural commodities during major crises, particularly for soybeans. These findings offer valuable insights into commodity market integration, portfolio diversification, and hedging strategies under extreme market conditions.

title: Reconciling Consumer and Vendor Preferences for Food Safety Attributes in Dhaka Wet Markets, Bangladesh
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, independent consultant, The Kenya National Treasury, CGIAR - International Potato Center, CGIAR - International Potato Center, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and CGIAR - International Potato Center

detail.title: Reconciling Consumer and Vendor Preferences for Food Safety Attributes in Dhaka Wet Markets, Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization presents major challenges to urban food systems, impacting access to safe and nutritious food especially in developing countries. With the urban demand for food surging, there is a proliferation of largely unregulated vendors in the informal food sector to meet this demand. However, these vendors often work in market environments characterized by inadequate sanitation infrastructure and poor waste management processes. Coupled with low consumer and vendor awareness on food safety, this presents a high risk for the spread of foodborne diseases and a significant threat to public health. To understand both demand-and supply-side policy options for promoting food safety, this study utilizes a choice experiment approach to investigate the interplay between consumer preferences and vendor practices regarding food safety in Dhaka's urban markets. The study finds that consumers favour high-quality fresh produce and prioritize vendors with good hygiene, as well as markets with medium to high sanitation. Conversely, vendors have high preferences for markets with improved sanitation and permanent infrastructure, but show hesitation towards investments in storage improvements, underlining the need for targeted policy interventions. Both consumers and vendors have a high willingness to pay for improved market conditions that promote food quality and safety, suggesting that improving market sanitation infrastructure and establishing permanent structures to maintain the quality of fresh produce could be mutually beneficial for both types of actors. Additionally, enhancing food safety awareness among both parties is imperative, addressing the prevalent disregard for vendor hygiene and its repercussions for public health.

title: From Delivery Apps to Courtrooms: The Struggle to Define Gig Work in India
affiliations: Nirma University, Institute of Law and Institute of Law, Nirma University

detail.title: From Delivery Apps to Courtrooms: The Struggle to Define Gig Work in India
detail.abstract: India’s food and grocery delivery apps such as Zomato, Swiggy, Blinkit, Zepto, and BigBasket have changed the rhythm of urban life. Every quick delivery tells two stories, the story of convenience for the customer and the story of struggle for the worker making it happen. These gig workers, who are often celebrated as symbols of digital progress, continue to work without job security, social benefits, or fair protection. The Code on Social Security, 2020, was expected to bridge this gap but has so far offered only limited relief. Adding to this challenge is the control of algorithms that decide who gets orders, how much they earn, and whether they can continue to work at all. This blog explores how the law can catch up with the new realities of digital labour, and why fairness and dignity must be central to India’s growing gig economy.

title: The Job Posting-Hiring Gap: Empirical Evidence and Theoretical Insights into its Causes and Consequences

detail.title: The Job Posting-Hiring Gap: Empirical Evidence and Theoretical Insights into its Causes and Consequences
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of online recruitment has transformed how organizations signal labor demand and how policymakers gauge workforce dynamics. Yet, a growing discrepancy exists between the number of online job postings and realized hiring outcomes-a phenomenon termed the Job Posting-Hiring Gap (JPHG). Drawing on Canadian labor market data from February to August 2025, this study provides empirical evidence that postings on major platforms such as LinkedIn and Indeed substantially overstate actual employment growth. On average, employment declined slightly even as vacancy volumes rose, indicating that a significant proportion of postings do not correspond to genuine hiring activity. To explain this divergence, the paper integrates established theories in organizational and labor market research. It identifies organizational, strategic, and labor market mechanisms-such as brand signaling, pipeline maintenance, and monopsonistic frictions-that generate the gap, as well as mediators like employer attractiveness and matching efficiency. The consequences extend beyond data distortion: for job seekers, the JPHG fosters fatigue and distrust; for firms, it introduces reputational and operational inefficiencies; and for policymakers, it undermines the reliability of vacancy statistics as indicators of labor demand. By combining empirical and theoretical evidence, the study establishes the JPHG as a structural feature of digitalized labor markets and calls for a reconsideration of how vacancy data are interpreted in human resource management, organizational research, and macroeconomic policy.

title: BRICS: A Potential Challenge to The U.S. Dollar Dominance

detail.title: BRICS: A Potential Challenge to The U.S. Dollar Dominance
detail.abstract: This research paper delves into the shifting realignments of global power structures within the framework of the New World Order, focusing on the diplomatic coalition of BRICS and its potential threat for the U.S. dollar dominance. The global transformation arise from three major crises the 2008 financial crisis, the Covid-19 crisis, and most recently the energy and commodity challenges in the aftermath of Russia-Ukrain war. These events led to a shared conviction thatthe form of monetary framework, pursued over the past decade is no longer sustainable. Consequently, a paradigm shift is underway, leading towards multolateralism through the emergence of three major hubs of globalisation. One controlled by the U.S. and North America. Western Europe is the second and Asia, dominated by China is third in the row. Therefore, it became very crucial for the global south to redefine their positions in this new geo-economic map either as a satellite or a strategic partner to the rest of the global economy. Traditonally, future of the International system is perceived through two assumptions: first, that emerging powers would integrate themselves into the existing global governance framework, and second, U.S. led institutions would be would remain dominant. However, the BRICS nations, have been forming revisionist alliances and establishing new institutions, challenging the dominant role of the U.S. in global affairs. The research is structured as follows: The initial section introduces the BRICS and The Existing Monitory Framework. Subsequent sections delve into the analytical framework in the context of pathways for BRICS towards de-dollarization, the evolution of BRICS, possible challenges for BRICS towards de-dollarization, its impact on the status quo, and the US response. The concluding part summarizes key insights and provides recommendations for future possibilities.

title: Geopolitical Risks and Energy Prices: Impacts of Russia-Ukraine Conflict
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Geopolitical Risks and Energy Prices: Impacts of Russia-Ukraine Conflict
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict on domestic energy prices across 85 countries using a structural factor-augmented vector autoregression framework. The main innovation is the construction of a conflict-specific shock from the common component of geopolitical risks in Russia and Ukraine, enabling a precise identification of the direct risk channel versus indirect global channels. The findings reveal a significant heterogeneity across countries in the transmission of shocks. For highly exposed European nations like Moldova, Austria, and Latvia, the direct geopolitical risk channel is a primary driver of energy price volatility, accounting for 20-25% of price fluctuations. In contrast, for major economies like Germany and the United States, impacts of the conflict are transmitted indirectly, with global economic activity and world oil prices explaining over 50% of energy price movements. The analysis provides a causally identified account of how a major geopolitical event propagates through the global economy.

title: Licensing Negotiation Groups: The New Antitrust Kid on the SEPs Block
affiliations: Università degli Studi della Basilicata

detail.title: Licensing Negotiation Groups: The New Antitrust Kid on the SEPs Block
detail.abstract: The European approach to standard essential patent (SEP) licensing increasingly resembles a form of therapeutic obstinacy. Even before the Draft Regulation was definitively withdrawn, a new issue had already taken center stage in the policy debate. As part of the ongoing review of the Technology Transfer Block Exemption Regulation (TTBER) and the related Guidelines (TTGs), the European Commission is considering providing guidance on the competition law assessment of licensing negotiation groups (LNGs). The recent draft revision of the TTGs, which was preceded by an informal guidance letter concerning the establishment of the Automotive Licensing Negotiation Group, illustrates the Commission's responsiveness to implementers' concerns. Thus, in what feels like a Groundhog Day, the same arguments, justifications, and objectives that were hotly debated in connection with the Draft Regulation have resurfaced. Indeed, much like the rationale underlying the SEP regulatory proposal, a favourable antitrust assessment of LNGs is intended to address a perceived holdup problem by promoting a solution that redistributes value from SEP holders to implementers. Against this backdrop, the paper examines these implementers' alliances under competition law and explores their implications within the current SEP licensing framework.

title: Does the Search for Stability Compromise Bank Competition?
affiliations: Brunel University London, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University

detail.title: Does the Search for Stability Compromise Bank Competition?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the short and long run effects of macroprudential policies on banks competition in two distinct markets: traditional intermediation and fee based activities. Drawing on the experience of Asian banking systems between the Asian Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a novel adaptation of Bolt and Humphrey’s competition–efficiency model that enables us to distinguish between the competition determinants across different markets and time horizons. Our results are robust to alternative specifications and reveal that banks adjust quickly in the short run, when competition is relatively high, but that frequent policy changes are costly in the long run as they increase uncertainty. We also find that effects vary in magnitude and direction across markets, highlighting the need for market-specific policy design and careful calibration of reform timing.

title: Optimal Capital Taxation with Borrowing Constraints and Entrepreneurial Heterogeneity
affiliations: Università di Roma "Tor Vergata", University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and LUISS Guido Carli - Department of Economics

detail.title: Optimal Capital Taxation with Borrowing Constraints and Entrepreneurial Heterogeneity

publicationDetails.journalName: CEIS: Centre for Economic & International Studies Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the optimal taxation of labor and various forms of capital in a model with entrepreneurial heterogeneity and financial frictions as in Itskhoki and Moll (2019a). We consider both a closed economy, populated by workers that buy corporate bonds, and a small open economy with hand-to-mouth workers where entrepreneurs finance capital by using their wealth and by borrowing abroad. The optimal fiscal policy differs depending on whether we consider the closed economy or the small open economy. In the former the taxes on labor and pure capital should be positive, while the tax on capital income should be zero. The wealth tax levied on workers and entrepreneurs and the pure capital tax levied on firms are equivalent fiscal instruments. When we consider a small open economy, we find that the pure capital tax should be set to zero but both the capital income tax and the labor tax should be positive. In this case the capital income tax and the wealth tax are perfect substitutes.

title: Beyond the Gender Binary: Wage Inequality and Occupational Segregation among Transgender and Nonbinary Workers
affiliations: , York University and Brock University

detail.title: Beyond the Gender Binary: Wage Inequality and Occupational Segregation among Transgender and Nonbinary Workers
detail.abstract: This study examines labor market disparities across gender identities in Canada using data from the 2021 Canadian Census, the first national census to identify transgender and nonbinary individuals. We analyze employment probabilities, work hours, and hourly wages among six gender groups: cisgender men, cisgender women, transgender men, transgender women, and nonbinary individuals assigned male or female at birth. Transgender and nonbinary individuals are 8-14 percentage points less likely to be employed than cisgender men and earn 20-30 percent lower hourly wages on average. After adjusting for demographic, occupational, and industrial characteristics, earnings gaps remain substantial-approximately 8-17 percentand are largest for nonbinary individuals assigned female at birth. Subgroup analyses reveal pronounced heterogeneity across occupations: wage gaps are smallest in health-related fields but largest in management and leadership positions, where gender minorities are also underrepresented. Transgender men fare relatively better in male-dominated fields such as trades and manufacturing, while nonbinary individuals show higher representation in arts and education. Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions indicate that about half of the overall wage gap is explained by differences in observable characteristics, with the remainder unexplained. The findings document persistent and uneven economic disadvantages for gender-diverse populations and highlight occupational contexts where barriers to inclusion are most pronounced.

title: Investor Behavior in the Pre-Opening: The Role of Price Impact and Strategic Interaction
affiliations: University of Siena - Department of Economics and Statistics

detail.title: Investor Behavior in the Pre-Opening: The Role of Price Impact and Strategic Interaction
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a framework for analyzing the portfolio strategies of investors who participate in the pre-opening and regular market sessions. Investors act strategically, recognizing that their pre-opening orders influence the asset's opening price. I examine the roles of key factors, such as the characteristics of price impact, number of market participants, investor heterogeneity, risk aversion, and the presence of retail investor, in shaping portfolio strategies and their implications for capital gains and stock price volatility during the regular trading session. The results shed light on the nuanced effects of the pre-opening session on the broader dynamics of financial markets.

title: Product Assortment Effects of Mergers
affiliations: Koc University

detail.title: Product Assortment Effects of Mergers
detail.abstract: The effect of mergers on product assortments is ambiguous. Reduced competition may disincentivize firms from offering a wide variety of options, while efficiency gains may lower the cost of introducing new offerings. This study empirically analyzes the impact of mergers on product assortments in the car rental industry using three cross-sections of airport-brand level data before and after the Hertz-Dollar Thrifty and Avis Budget-Payless mergers. The results indicate that mergers generally lead to a decreased growth in the number of car rental offerings, particularly for specialized vehicle types such as SUVs and vans, suggesting a decline in assortment diversity. However, this effect is not observed in larger markets, implying lower anti-competitive effects. The study discusses the policy implications for merger regulation, emphasizing the importance of considering market-specific factors.

title: Global Oil Prices and Metro Ridership in the Greater Manila Area: A Structural Vector Autoregression Analysis
affiliations: Asian Institute of Management, Asian Institute of Management and Asian Institute of Management

detail.title: Global Oil Prices and Metro Ridership in the Greater Manila Area: A Structural Vector Autoregression Analysis

declarations.funderStatement: This study is funded by Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung.

detail.abstract: Global oil price volatility has historically influenced economic stability, with major shocks in the 1970s, during the First Gulf War, and in 2008 driving global inflation. While developed economies often cushion these effects through efficient public transport systems, developing countries with informal and fragmented networks face greater vulnerability. Despite growing recognition of sustainable mobility’s role in reducing emissions and improving urban livability, limited research explores behavioral responses to oil price shocks in the Global South, particularly in Southeast Asia. This paper examines the impact of global oil price shocks on public transport ridership and macroeconomic variables in the Philippines using Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) analysis. Focusing on Metro Rail Transit (MRT) and Light Rail Transit (LRT) ridership in the Greater Manila Area from January 2005 to December 2019, the study analyzes the effects of a one-standard deviation increase in global oil prices. Results suggest a delayed but positive response in metro ridership, assuming gradual commuter shifts from private to public transport as fuel prices rise. By providing empirical evidence from a developing country context, this study contributes to understanding oil price shocks and transport behavior in the Global South.

title: A Global Systems Perspective on Food Demand, Deforestation and Agricultural Sustainability
affiliations: Ecole Polytechnique, Palaiseau, Ecole Polytechnique, Palaiseau, Capital Fund Management and Peking University - College of Urban and Environmental Sciences

detail.title: A Global Systems Perspective on Food Demand, Deforestation and Agricultural Sustainability
detail.abstract: Feeding a larger and wealthier global population without transgressing ecological limits is increasingly challenging, as rising food demand-especially for animal products-intensifies pressure on ecosystems, accelerates deforestation, and erodes biodiversity and soil health. We develop a stylized, spatially explicit global model that links exogenous food-demand trajectories to crop and livestock production, land conversion, and feedbacks from ecosystem integrity that, in turn, shape future yields and land needs. Calibrated to post-1960 trends in population, income, yields, input use, and land use, the model reproduces the joint rise of crop and meat demand and the associated expansion and intensification of agriculture. We use it to compare business-as-usual, supply-side, demand-side, and mixed-policy scenarios. Three results stand out. First, productivity-oriented supply-side measures (e.g. reduced chemical inputs, organic conversion, lower livestock density) often trigger compensatory land expansion that undermines ecological gains-so that supply-side action alone cannot halt deforestation or widespread degradation. Second, demand-side change, particularly reduced meat consumption, consistently relieves both intensification and expansion pressures; in our simulations, only substantial demand reductions (on the order of 40% of projected excess demand by 2100) deliver simultaneous increases in forest area and declines in degraded land. Third, integrated policy portfolios that jointly constrain land conversion, temper input intensification, and curb demand outperform any single lever. Together, these findings clarify the system-level trade-offs that frustrate piecemeal interventions and identify the policy combinations most likely to keep global food provision within ecological limits.

title: Flexible Work Arrangements (Flextime, Telecommuting, Compressed Workweeks) and Employee Productivity in Murang’a Level 5 Hospital
affiliations: Zetech University, Zetech University and Zetech University

detail.title: Flexible Work Arrangements (Flextime, Telecommuting, Compressed Workweeks) and Employee Productivity in Murang’a Level 5 Hospital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that this research was not influenced by anyone and it was my research project for completion of my masters degree.
declarations.ethicsApproval: I declare I got the approval to conduct this research through NACOSTI and individual participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was fully funded through my own savings and no organization provided any incentives.

detail.abstract: This study examined the relationship between employee productivity and flexible work arrangements (FWAs), such as compressed workweeks, flextime, and telecommuting at Murang'a Level 5 Hospital, a Kenyan rural public healthcare facility dealing with a high patient load and staff shortage challenges. Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Model, Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, and Social Exchange Theory were used. A mixed-methods approach was utilised, surveying 205 employees from a population of 421 selected through stratified sampling. SPSS was used to perform analysis for both qualitative and quantitative data, including thematic coding and multiple regression. Key findings from 186 respondents (90.7% response rate) showed that telecommuting (β = 0.176, p = 0.005), flextime (β = 0.421, p < 0.001), and compressed workweeks (β = 0.269, p < 0.001) had positive effects on employee productivity. The regression analysis yielded R² values of 0.046, 0.236, and 0.107, accounting for approximately 4.6%, 23.6% and 10.7% of the employee productivity variance, respectively. The findings informed hospital management, healthcare professionals, and policymakers on optimising hybrid FWAs to improved service delivery, aligning with Kenya's Vision 2030, Murang'a County 2022-2027 objectives, and Sustainable Development Goal 3. The study extended existing literature by demonstrating variations in FWA effectiveness across staff categories, with flextime showing stronger impacts in non-clinical roles compared to clinical ones, where physical presence limited telecommuting. This addressed a gap in Kenyan public hospitals, where previous research primarily focused on urban and nonhealthcare settings, and highlighted the significance of applying the findings to similar rural facilities while cautioning against direct generalization without considering local infrastructure.

title: The Role of Psychological Safety in Intelligent Business Systems of the Future -Implications and Implementation
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: The Role of Psychological Safety in Intelligent Business Systems of the Future -Implications and Implementation
detail.abstract: This paper explores the critical role of psychological safety in the development and operation of intelligent business systems (IBS) of the future. Psychological safety, defined as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, has shown to improve innovation, learning, and performance [1][2]. In IBS, where human-machine interaction is prominent, fostering psychological safety becomes vital to ensure seamless collaboration between employees and intelligent technologies [9][10]. The fast-paced evolution of AI-driven environments demands that employees feel secure in expressing ideas, raising concerns, and embracing experimentation without fear of judgment or reprisal [23]. A quantitative research methodology was employed involving a survey administered to 500 employees across multinational corporations that have adopted intelligent systems. Key constructs such as psychological safety, trust in AI, team collaboration, and perceived team performance were measured using a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = Strongly Disagree to 7 = Strongly Agree [29]. This format was chosen to capture the nuances of participants' perceptions across key constructs. Data analysis was conducted using structural equation modelling (SEM) to uncover the relationships among these variables. The findings reveal that psychological safety significantly enhances team collaboration and trust in AI, which in turn drive improved team performance in intelligent business environments [26]. These insights led to the development of the Integrated Psychological Safety in Intelligent Business Systems (IPS-IBS) Framework; a novel model designed to guide organizations in embedding psychological safety as a core principle within their intelligent systems strategy [23]. A visual representation of this framework is provided to support practical implementation and policy development.

title: Augmented Reality(AR) in the Classroom: Understanding How AR Enhances Traditional Learning Methods by Overlaying Digital Information onto the Physical World
affiliations: Jazan University and Jazan University

detail.title: Augmented Reality(AR) in the Classroom: Understanding How AR Enhances Traditional Learning Methods by Overlaying Digital Information onto the Physical World
detail.abstract: The present study is a literature review and analysis of research articles related to the implementation and impact of augmented reality in education. It involves synthesizing information from various scholarly sources to understand the current landscape, trends, and findings in the field of augmented reality in educational settings. This review delves into the revolutionary influence of Augmented Reality (AR) within educational settings, scrutinizing the trajectory of research from 2009 to 2023. By seamlessly overlaying digital content onto the physical world, AR emerges as a catalyst for reshaping conventional learning approaches. The examination involves a meticulous bibliometric assessment and empirical investigations, spotlighting a notable upswing in AR research publications, particularly in the educational landscapes of the United States and China. The focal points of scrutiny include technology, motivation, environment, games, interests, achievement, and development. The synthesis of findings not only illuminates critical facets but also addresses lacunae and outlines future research prospects within the realm of AR in education. This comprehensive review stands as a valuable compass for educators, researchers, and policymakers navigating the dynamic terrain of educational

title: Output Transparency: Differentiating Human and AI Creativity through Legal Reforms
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Output Transparency: Differentiating Human and AI Creativity through Legal Reforms
detail.abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has presented our legal system with a profound new dilemma. Public confidence in the capacity of AI to generate content is growing quickly, nearly apace with advancements in the technology itself. Yet, as AI-generated content masquerading as human-authored increasingly floods online platforms, our ability to tell the difference is diminishing. This widespread concealment of AI’s role in content creation has unleashed a cascade of harms for individuals as well as society at large. This article exposes the law’s failure to regulate AI concealment, a legal vacuum that permits the proliferation of such concealment. To address this challenge, we must first theoretically interrogate why it is important to distinguish AI-generated content from human-authored works. Building on this theoretical foundation, we can then consider the feasibility of adopting a robust legal standard to regulate AI concealment. To this end, the article advances a theory of “differentiated creativity”. This theory clarifies the fundamental differences between human creative processes—rooted in human intentionality, emotional expression, and control—and those of AI. Based on this theory, the article then proposes “output transparency” as a new legal standard enabling clear differentiation between human and AI contributions. To operationalize output transparency, the article advocates two key legal reforms: requiring technology companies to watermark AI-generated content, and obligating authors to provide proper explanations of the modifications they have made to such content. These proposed reforms would protect human adaptations of AI outputs, ensure a clear distinction between human and machine contributions, and enhance transparency across creative sectors. By implementing these reforms, the legal system can more effectively safeguard and foster the creative potential of both humans and AI, promoting balanced and ethical integration of technology in society.

title: Quantum Machine Learning – The Black Swan and Grey Rhino Problem : Are we Building the Next Financial Crisis?
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: Quantum Machine Learning – The Black Swan and Grey Rhino Problem : Are we Building the Next Financial Crisis?
detail.abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing have demonstrated improved performance in financial prediction tasks, with IBM and HSBC reporting a 34% improvement in algorithmic trading fill probability predictions. However, analysis of the published results reveals a concerning pattern: quantum circuits with inherent Gaussian-like noise characteristics systematically smooth input distributions, progressively eliminating the fat-tailed features that signal rare, high-impact market events. This paper examines the structural parallels between this tail-filtering mechanism and the pre-2008 financial crisis, when Value-at-Risk models similarly optimised for Gaussian assumptions whilst systematically underestimating catastrophic tail risk. Drawing on Taleb's theory of fat-tailed distributions and the concept of Grey Rhino events (predictable but ignored threats), I argue that quantum-enhanced machine learning may replicate the exact failure mode that contributed to systemic collapse in 2008. The evidence for this tail-filtering effect is visible in IBM-HSBC's own published histograms, which show progressive Gaussianisation with increased circuit depth. Whilst quantum ML researchers and financial institutions have likely considered these implications, this paper documents the observable warning signs to discharge an epistemic obligation: if quantumenhanced models exhibit catastrophic failures during future market stress events, the mechanism will have been identified, and the pattern will have been visible in the data from the outset.

title: Shaping psychologists' professional identity during a period of crisis: An existential-dialectical approach
affiliations: Riga Stradins University, Riga Stradins University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Shaping psychologists' professional identity during a period of crisis: An existential-dialectical approach
detail.abstract: This study explored how the professional identity of psychologists was shaped during the crisis period characterised by the COVID-19 pandemic, accelerated digitalisation, and the war in Ukraine. Drawing on an existential-dialectical framework, the research examined how psychologists navigated practical contradictions and existential tensions involving meaning, purpose, and professional significance during widespread disruption. The qualitative study included 45 experienced Latvian psychologists (M = 47.13 years, 87% women) who began practising before the pandemic. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews conducted in October-November 2022. Reflexive thematic analysis was employed to identify patterns of professional identity transformation, with particular attention to dialectical tensions and existential challenges. Five themes emerged: (1) reconciling traditional practices with crisis-driven changes, where remote work created boundary challenges while proving effective; (2) balancing emotional vulnerability and professional responsibility, as rising demand intensified both strain and professional value; (3) navigating isolation and collaboration through enhanced supervision and peer support; (4) evolving professional practices through creativity and functional adaptations; and (5) experiencing professional growth through strengthened commitment despite initial uncertainty. The findings demonstrate that professional identity transformation during crises involves navigating universal dialectical tensions while addressing existential challenges of meaning and purpose. Psychologists adaptively integrated reflective practices, digital competencies, and self-care strategies. The study contributes to professional identity literature by demonstrating that crises serve as catalysts for comprehensive identity transformation, fostering more adaptive, reflective, and resilient professional identities through resolving both practical contradictions and existential uncertainties.

title: ChatGPT Referrals to E-Commerce Websites: Do LLMs Outperform Traditional Channels?
affiliations: University of Hamburg and

detail.title: ChatGPT Referrals to E-Commerce Websites: Do LLMs Outperform Traditional Channels?
detail.abstract: We investigate the performance of organic Large Language Model traffic (oLLM) versus traditional digital channels in e-commerce. Analyzing 12 months of first-party data from 973 websites with $20 billion combined revenue, we examine over 50,000 transactions from ChatGPT referrals alongside 164 million transactions from traditional channels. Using regression models that account for data sparsity, we assess financial metrics (conversion rate, average order value, revenue per session) and engagement metrics (bounce rate, session duration, page views). Results contradict widespread expectations of oLLM superiority. Organic LLM traffic underperforms all traditional channels except paid social media across key financial metrics. While oLLM achieves favorable bounce rates, indicating relevance, it generates lower conversion rates and revenue per session than Google's paid and organic search channels. The performance gap persists across extensive robustness checks varying aggregation periods, observation thresholds, and website samples. Despite current underperformance, oLLM shows positive trajectories. Conversion rates improved over the observation period, though declining average order values offset some gains. Time-trend analyses suggest gradual convergence with traditional channels, but projections indicate oLLM will not achieve parity with organic search within the next year. These findings challenge narratives of LLMs as immediate "Google killers" while suggesting potential for long-term channel evolution.

title: Republic Act No. 11058
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Republic Act No. 11058
detail.abstract: This paper provides a critical analysis of Republic Act No. 11058, also known as the Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) Law of 2018. The study examines the law’s objectives, key provisions, strengths, and weaknesses in ensuring safe and healthy working conditions for Filipino workers. RA 11058 institutionalizes safety compliance by mandating employers to provide proper training, equipment, and hazard prevention systems, while also empowering workers to uphold their rights. Despite its progressive framework, the implementation of the law faces challenges such as limited inspection capacity of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), financial burdens on small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and low awareness among informal workers. The analysis concludes that while RA 11058 significantly advances labor protection in the Philippines, greater institutional support, awareness campaigns, and incentives for compliance are needed to achieve its full potential in promoting workplace safety and productivity.

title: The Impact of Workplace Psychological Violence on the Safety Attitude of Operating Room Nurses: The Mediation of Psychological Resilience
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Workplace Psychological Violence on the Safety Attitude of Operating Room Nurses: The Mediation of Psychological Resilience
detail.abstract: Background: Workplace psychological violence erodes OR nurses’ professional identity, fuels burnout and threatens patient safety. Psychological resilience may buffer these effects, yet its role in linking violence to safety attitudes remains unclear. Methods: A 2024 cross-sectional survey recruited 296 OR nurses from seven Shanghai tertiary hospitals. Participants completed the WPVB, CD-RISC and SAQ-OR instruments. Spearman correlations and Process Model 4 were used to test the mediating effect of resilience on the violence–attitude pathway. Results: Higher violence exposure was associated with lower resilience (r = –0.363) and poorer safety attitudes (r = –0.313), whereas resilience strongly predicted better attitudes (r = 0.500). Resilience accounted for 47.7 % of the total effect of violence on safety attitudes. Conclusion: Psychological violence is prevalent among OR nurses; strengthening resilience and a positive safety culture may mitigate its detrimental impact on safety performance.
