The qualitative study included 45 experienced Latvian psychologists (M = 47.13 years, 87% women) who began practising before the pandemic. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews conducted in October-November 2022. Reflexive thematic analysis was employed to identify patterns of professional identity transformation, with particular attention to dialectical tensions and existential challenges. Five themes emerged: (1) reconciling traditional practices with crisis-driven changes, where remote work created boundary challenges while proving effective; (2) balancing emotional vulnerability and professional responsibility, as rising demand intensified both strain and professional value; (3) navigating isolation and collaboration through enhanced supervision and peer support; (4) evolving professional practices through creativity and functional adaptations; and (5) experiencing professional growth through strengthened commitment despite initial uncertainty. The findings demonstrate that professional identity transformation during crises involves navigating universal dialectical tensions while addressing existential challenges of meaning and purpose. Psychologists adaptively integrated reflective practices, digital competencies, and self-care strategies. The study contributes to professional identity literature by demonstrating that crises serve as catalysts for comprehensive identity transformation, fostering more adaptive, reflective, and resilient professional identities through resolving both practical contradictions and existential uncertainties.

title: Platform Certification and Seller Disclosure in Online Selling
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Platform Certification and Seller Disclosure in Online Selling
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Concern about product quality due to the inability to experience products physically has been a major factor that hinders consumers from purchasing online. To ease such concerns, online platforms and sellers have been engaged in various activities to reveal product quality information. Platform can provide certification to products sold via its marketplace, while sellers can voluntarily disclose their private quality information. Despite platform certification and seller disclosure being prevalent quality information revelation methods, the interaction between them has been seldom examined. In this study, we develop a game-theoretical model to analytically explore the implications of platform certification and seller disclosure in an online selling context. Methodology/results: We consider a continuum of sellers offering new products to end consumers through an online platform under one of two pricing schemes: (1) pay-per-transaction (commission fees) or (2) pay-per-listing (listing fees). Consumers hold prior beliefs about product quality and update them based on the observed platform certification and seller disclosure behavior. Our analysis shows that under the commission fee scheme, platform certification serves an informational role by influencing sellers' disclosure strategies and enhancing consumers' ability to infer quality. Platform certification always benefits the platform but may either benefit or hurt sellers, depending on their quality levels. Under the listing fee scheme, platform certification instead serves an enrollment role: the platform sets a certification standard to enhance consumers' quality expectation towards nondisclosure sellers, thereby encouraging more sellers to participate in online selling. In this case, platform certification continues to benefit the platform but does not affect sellers' disclosure behavior or profitability. We further demonstrate that our main findings remain robust across various alternative model specifications. Managerial implications: Our analysis reveals that the interplay between platform certification and seller disclosure generates non-trivial effects for both platforms and sellers. Platforms should carefully design its certification strategies in alignment with pricing structures, while sellers should adjust their disclosure strategies in response to platform certification decisions.

title: Minimum Wages and Employment
affiliations: Arizona State University W. P. Carey School of Business and  Arizona State University (ASU), W.P. Carey School of Business, Students

detail.title: Minimum Wages and Employment
detail.abstract: Minimum wages do not necessarily cause a reduction in employment as fundamental microeconomics principles suggest. In the food and agriculture industry, minimum wages may be important tools to not only address income inequalities, but to increase the quantity of labor supplied and potentially help solve chronic labor shortages. While there are many possible explanations for the paradox of minimum wage neutrality, from correcting for monopsony power to segmented labor markets, we examine a relatively new and important mechanism. Namely, we test for whether minimum wages have a "cleansing" effect in industries that tend to employ minimum-wage workers, driving relatively inefficient firms, or those that could only survive by paying workers low wages, out of the industry. Exiting firms cede market share to more efficient firms, who employ the workers that are released by the exiting firms. We examine this question using a two-stage approach, first using reduced-form methods in aggregate data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) and then using micro-level data on individual firms in the retail industry from NielsenIQ TDLinx data set. We find broad support for the cleansing hypothesis in both the aggregate and micro-level analyses, suggesting that minimum wages may have a beneficial efficiency-enhancing effect that has otherwise been overlooked in the policy literature.

reference: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 558
title: Industry Contribution to U.S. Wage Inequality

detail.title: Industry Contribution to U.S. Wage Inequality

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 558
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management & Statistics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Industry dimension is increasingly dominant to investigate the upward trend of inequality. This paper examines the key drivers of U.S. wage inequality through a general equilibrium model, emphasising the role of heterogeneous capital-labour substitution elasticities across industries in shaping wage dispersion. Key is the distinction of a quantity effect (changes in the composition of capital and labour inputs) and a structural effect (reflecting technological transformations in inputs substitutability) from Skill-Biased Technological Change (SBTC). Findings suggest that industry-level transformations on the labour sidedifferentials in job tasks substitutability and workforce compositionconstitute the principal drivers of real wage inequality, overshadowing the contribution of capital-side adjustments. A structural estimation of the model reveals that trend-asymmetries in the elasticities of substitution between ICT capital, routine and non-routine workers account for 94% of observed wage variance, while stronger sorting and segregation effects further exacerbate such dispersion. Upon neutralising structural differences between industries, SBTC reckons merely 6-15% of the observed wage inequality.

title: Coalition Government in South Africa: The Political Solution
affiliations: Durban University of Technology, Durban University of Technology, University of South Africa (UNISA) and University of South Africa (UNISA)

detail.title: Coalition Government in South Africa: The Political Solution
detail.abstract:
This paper explores coalition government in South Africa as a potential solution to governance challenges in a diverse society. As the nation faces political fragmentation, economic inequality, and social unrest, traditional party politics often fall short of addressing citizen needs. The study argues that coalition governments offer a more inclusive framework, fostering collaboration among various political parties and interest groups.

The research examines the historical context of coalition politics in South Africa, particularly in the post-apartheid political landscape. This paper analyses recent electoral trends leading to increased party fragmentation, where no single party secures an outright majority, necessitating coalition formation through negotiated agreements among diverse political actors.

Using thirty-one relevant articles on historical precedents from 2001 - 2025, current trends, and case studies of coalition governments at national and provincial levels, the paper assesses the benefits and challenges of this governance model. Successful examples illustrate how coalitions can facilitate inclusive policymaking and improve service delivery, while potential pitfalls include instability and conflicting agendas among partners.

Additionally, the study discusses the role of civil society and community engagement in supporting coalition governments, emphasizing transparency, accountability, and public participation in decision-making. In conclusion, the paper posits that coalition government may be a viable political solution for South Africa, addressing the complexities of its multifaceted society. By fostering cooperation among diverse political actors, coalitions can enhance governance, promote social cohesion, and contribute to a more equitable and democratic South Africa. The findings aim to inform policymakers, political analysts, and stakeholders about the transformative potential of coalition governance in the country

reference: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 559
title: The Horizontal Geometry of Production Networks

detail.title: The Horizontal Geometry of Production Networks

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management and Statistics Working Paper No. 559
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Milan Bicocca Department of Economics, Management & Statistics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Complementarities in intermediate inputs trigger the even transmission of asymmetric shocks in production networks. This paper linearly captures these complementarities through shared inter-sectoral trade relationships, and makes two novel contributions to the understanding of networked economies. First, it introduces a theoretical framework that distinguishes between factor input demand and factor input supply network distances, measuring economic distance between sectors based on common upstream sellers or downstream buyers. These horizontal interdependencies determine how sector-specific shocks transmit horizontally across the network, complementing and balancing the standard vertical (Leontief inverse) mechanism. Second, using sector-level U.S. employment data, the paper provides empirical evidence that positive employment shocks in closely demand-or supply-connected sectors are attenuated, whereas larger distances generate employment comovement. Together, these two contributions reveal that the horizontal geometry of a production network plays a critical role in understanding how sectoral interactions propagate micro-originated shocks in an Input-Output economy.

title: Research on RA 9003: Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Research on RA 9003: Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
detail.abstract:
Abstract

This paper discusses Republic Act No. 9003, also known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, which serves as a major environmental law in the Philippines. Enacted to promote proper waste management, the law emphasizes shared responsibility among individuals, communities, and government agencies in reducing, segregating, and disposing of waste properly. It sets clear objectives: protecting public health, raising environmental awareness, and promoting recycling and ecological practices such as composting and segregation at the source.

The study outlines key provisions, including waste segregation, the establishment of Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs), the prohibition of harmful waste disposal practices, and the enforcement of penalties for violations. It also highlights the role of the National Solid Waste Management Commission and the requirement for local governments to create 10-year waste management plans.

Despite its significance, the paper notes that implementation remains a challenge due to weak enforcement, lack of funding, and limited public participation. Strengthening community involvement, improving facilities, and enforcing the law more strictly are identified as essential steps toward success. Ultimately, RA 9003 is a vital tool for achieving sustainable development and ensuring a cleaner and healthier environment for future generations.

title: Convergence
affiliations: University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: Convergence
detail.abstract:
In recent years, the United States has mobilized a vast regulatory machine to stunt China’s growth and curb its competitiveness. Departing from prevailing economic and political science literature that examines why the United States seeks to contain China, this Article investigates how it pursues that objective and, crucially, what consequences these strategies have produced. Drawing on systems theory, it offers the first comprehensive account of the institutional pattern underpinning the legal architecture governing U.S. restrictions on trade, technology, data, and talent flows with China.

A central insight is convergence: in seeking to curb China’s rise, the United States has increasingly come to resemble its rival across three core dimensions of regulatory governance: structure, process, and outcome. Structurally, decision-making has become increasingly concentrated in the executive branch, which has stretched the boundaries of statutory authority through novel and expansive interpretations. Procedurally, policymaking has grown volatile—driven as much by partisan and personal interests as by shifting calculations of national interest. These dynamics have produced mixed results, while noisy market signals have delayed meaningful feedback about policy effectiveness.

This Article also advances a theory of convergence that explains the dynamic interactions between the two great powers. In response to strong domestic demand for tougher measures toward China, U.S. presidents adopt sweeping precautionary measures with limited cost–benefit analysis; those measures, in turn, intensify demand and generate powerful institutional momentum toward further containment. Beijing doubles down on self-sufficiency, narrowing technological gaps despite severe U.S. restrictions. As China grows more resilient, it demonstrates greater capacity and resolve to mount aggressive retaliation. Chinese countermeasures prompt the executive to undertake unprecedented, intrusive state intervention, further entrenching the expansion of presidential power.

As a result, absent a fundamental reorientation of the constitutional order governing foreign affairs and national security, U.S. legal containment will only accelerate convergence with China—a trajectory that carries profound implications not only for the future of U.S.–China rivalry but also for the United States’ own constitutional order.

title: Special Conference Calls
affiliations: New York Institute of Technology and Wayne State University - Mike Ilitch School of Business

detail.title: Special Conference Calls
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the determinants, content, and consequences of special conference calls. Special conference calls, meetings held by publicly-traded companies in which executives provide an overview of specific events related to the firm, have increased in frequency by 375% since the COVID-19 pandemic. Using 11,692 special calls held by U.S. public firms from 2005 to 2022, we find that hosting decisions are related to firm-level uncertainty and investor information demand. Firms that are larger, covered by more analysts, and operating in more complex business segments are more likely to hold these events. Equity markets treat special calls as incrementally informative relative to 8-Ks, with significantly positive abnormal returns and trading volume. Textual analysis of transcripts using latent Dirichlet allocation identifies four main topics: customer and growth discussions, strategic outcomes, biotech-related business updates, and clinical trial announcements. Market reactions differ across topics, with positive responses to growth and negative responses to trial announcements. A robustness analysis using BERTopic confirms these findings. Overall, special calls represent an important discretionary disclosure channel.

title: Behavioral Finance and Investor Psychology in Volatile Markets: Insights into Decision-Making, Biases, and Market Dynamics
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Behavioral Finance and Investor Psychology in Volatile Markets: Insights into Decision-Making, Biases, and Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of behavioral biases on investor decision-making within financial markets, particularly under conditions of volatility and uncertainty. It synthesizes insights from behavioral finance, psychology, neuroscience, and sociology to elucidate how cognitive heuristics, emotional responses, and social dynamics contribute to market inefficiencies and price anomalies. Key biases such as loss aversion, overconfidence, anchoring, availability, and herd behavior are analyzed in the context of their amplification during turbulent periods, with attention to cultural and regional variations. The work explores the interplay between individual psychological factors and collective phenomena, including contagion and synchronized trading patterns, highlighting the role of information dissemination through digital platforms and social media. It further discusses mitigation strategies encompassing investor education, decision-support tools, structured investment approaches, and regulatory interventions informed by behavioral principles. The integration of neuroscientific findings offers a biological perspective on the mechanisms underlying these biases, informing the design of more effective models and policies. The paper also addresses ethical considerations related to exploiting behavioral tendencies and emphasizes the responsibilities of financial advisors in guiding clients through complex market environments. Overall, the research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and managing the behavioral dimensions of investment, with implications for enhancing market stability and investor outcomes across diverse global contexts.

title: Nice Work if You Can Get it? The Distribution of Employment and Earnings during the Early Years of the Clean Energy Transition *
affiliations: University of Virginia, U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Census Bureau

detail.title: Nice Work if You Can Get it? The Distribution of Employment and Earnings during the Early Years of the Clean Energy Transition *
detail.abstract: The transition to clean energy represents a fundamental and important shift in economic activity. We present new facts about workers in clean and legacy energy sectors between 2005 and 2019 using linked, administrative employer-employee data for all W-2 workers in the United States. We show that both clean and legacy energy establishments hire a disproportionate share of non-Hispanic White and male workers compared to the working population, that workers rarely move from legacy to clean firms, and that, conditional on education, workers do not earn more in clean firms than in legacy firms. The occupational categories of jobs at clean firms differ notably from occupations at legacy firms and, on average, tend to be performed by workers with higher levels of education. Regional overlap in employment opportunities is not sufficient to facilitate worker transitions from legacy to clean firms. Substantially lower earnings outside of the energy sector combined with low mobility between legacy and clean firms suggests that the costs of the clean transition on workers in legacy fossil fuel sectors may be substantial. At the same time workers moving into clean activities from outside of the energy sector experience significant increases in earnings and greater job stability, suggesting that clean jobs are "good jobs" for those who can access them.

title: NavSense:Real-Time Spatial Awareness for the Visually Impaired Using LiDAR, Depth Cameras, and AI-based object detection
affiliations: K.J. Somaiya College of Engineering Somaiya Vidyavihar University, K. J. Somaiya College of Engineering and University of Mumbai - K. J. Somaiya College of Engineering (K.J.S.C.E.)

detail.title: NavSense:Real-Time Spatial Awareness for the Visually Impaired Using LiDAR, Depth Cameras, and AI-based object detection
detail.abstract: Indoor navigation poses immense challenges for visually impaired people in terms of requiring real-time spatial perception and obstacle detection for safe and independent mobility. This work proposes a state-of-the-art multimodal sensor fusion indoor navigation system consisting of YD LiDAR for 360 °horizontal mapping, two TF-Luna LiDARs for localized distance measurement, an Intel RealSense D435i depth camera to enable 3D spatial awareness and RGB imaging and AI-based object detection. The main indoor landmarks such as doors, stairs, exit signs, and people are identified by a custom YOLOv5-based neural network, ensuring intelligent decision making for navigation. The system integrates depth, LiDAR, and RGB inputs to create an intelligent real-time obstacle detection model that identifies potential hazards. A text-to-speech (TTS) feedback mechanism offers adaptive audio feedback aimed at enabling high-priority presentation of critical warnings (e.g. near collisions) over general navigational announcements. The architecture incorporates a training framework that aims to constantly reduce object detection error by accumulating labeled data and optimizing models. This proposed system offers real-time hands-free guidance, with the addition of multisensor fusion, deep learning, and adaptive auditory feedback making it easier to navigate unfamiliar indoor spaces. By blending data from multiple sensors, it improves environmental awareness, empowering visually impaired users to move safely and independently. Future work will show the application of Edge AI, adaptive learning models, and user adaptability to facilitate greater practical usability. This work will help advance AI-driven assistive technology towards next-generation smart mobility solutions.

title: Deep Analysis of the Balanced Free Trade Model with Quota System: Expanding on a Smarter Alternative to Tariffs for American Growth

detail.title: Deep Analysis of the Balanced Free Trade Model with Quota System: Expanding on a Smarter Alternative to Tariffs for American Growth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to influence the research or conclusions of this paper. The study was conducted independently and without institutional affiliation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research does not involve human subjects or data requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All analysis and preparation were completed independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a detailed analysis of the Balanced Free Trade Model with Quota System (BFT Model), expanding on the author’s original policy study, Balanced Free Trade Model with Quota System: A Smarter Alternative to Tariffs for American Growth [1]. Developed as a novel framework by the author, the BFT Model offers a lawful and economically efficient replacement for tariff-based trade policy. Whereas tariffs impose hidden taxes on American consumers, fuel inflation, and fail to eliminate trade deficits, the BFT Model directly addresses structural imbalances by requiring surplus countries to purchase quota rights equivalent to their surpluses. This mechanism ensures balanced trade, stable consumer prices, and substantial federal revenue without shifting costs onto U.S. families. Through historical data, legal analysis, and case studies of recent U.S. trade agreements with Japan and the European Union [3][4], this paper demonstrates why tariffs have consistently failed and why the BFT Model presents a superior alternative for sustainable American growth.

title: Pay More for Less Value: Cost of Conversion and Ad Relevance
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University (NYU), Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Department of Marketing, Students,  and New York University (NYU) - Department of Marketing

detail.title: Pay More for Less Value: Cost of Conversion and Ad Relevance
detail.abstract: We document a puzzling negative correlation between cost per conversion and conversion rate across industries in digital advertising, contradicting the standard expectation that higher conversion rates should command higher costs. To explain this phenomenon, we develop a model of a digital advertising platform featuring three players, advertiser, publisher, and consumers, where ad relevance influences both conversion and pricing outcomes. In the baseline model where the publisher determines ad relevance, we show that if the publisher gains an additional benefit from providing highly relevant ads, it may charge lower prices for more relevant ads even though they yield higher conversion rates. This mechanism generates a negative correlation between cost per conversion and conversion rate. The relationship emerges only when the publisher's benefit from relevance exceeds a threshold and remains robust when the advertiser, instead of the publisher, controls and pays for ad relevance. When advertisers set relevance, the publisher may even offer negative fees to encourage higher ad relevance. Our results help explain the counterintuitive phenomenon, providing new insights into the dynamics of digital advertising markets.

title: Implicit Government Guarantees and Corporate Risk-Taking: Evidence from SOE Defaults in China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Rhode Island - College of Business, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Implicit Government Guarantees and Corporate Risk-Taking: Evidence from SOE Defaults in China
detail.abstract: This study investigates how State-Owned Enterprises’ (SOEs) risk-taking behaviors change in response to reduced government guarantees in China. We find that SOEs significantly reduce their risk-taking activities following the first SOE default event in their respective provinces. Our analysis reveals three mechanisms that could explain this risk shift: reduced R&D spending, decreased holdings in risky financial assets, and increased working capital reserves. We also demonstrate the risk reduction intensifies when SOEs’ local governments face financial constraints and economic uncertainty. Our findings shed light on the intricate interplay between government support and corporate financial strategies.

title: Worst-Case Duration
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Worst-Case Duration
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new duration measure based on a worst-case forward rate shift in a Hilbert space. The norm is chosen so that the new measure is comparable to the standard duration interpreted as a directional derivative. The worst-case duration measure has many interesting and useful properties. In particular, like the standard duration, the worst-case duration is bounded by the cash flow payment dates and equals the time to maturity for a zero coupon bond. Empirical analysis using 35 years of weekly data highlights the robustness and effectiveness of this measure across a range of scenarios.

title: Pricing natural-disasters and climate-change risks: Insights from CAPM with self and externally excited jumps
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Polytechnic University of Turin - Dipartimento di Matematica

detail.title: Pricing natural-disasters and climate-change risks: Insights from CAPM with self and externally excited jumps
detail.abstract: We study the effect of climate change on market's risk premium and stock volatility through a general equilibrium asset pricing model with recursive preferences. We consider a financial market affected by environmental and macroeconomic shocks, both featuring time-varying intensities. Additionally, we incorporate the effects of green policies specifically targeting carbon-intensive assets. To capture the increasing frequency and clustering behavior of environmental risks, the model includes self-exciting and externally excited jump intensities for natural rare disasters. The representative agent's consumption-investment maximization problem is solved in closed form, and the analytical results suggest that consumption disasters with time-varying probability reduce the risk-free interest rates while increasing the market's premium and volatility of the stock market. The asymmetric impact of the transition risk on assets affects the optimal portfolio composition. Neglecting the clustering-like nature of environmental shocks lead to underestimate these effects.

title: Tech-Driven Redress: The Impact of Generative AI on Consumer Complaints in Financial Firms
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Keele University - Keele Business School and Florida Atlantic University

detail.title: Tech-Driven Redress: The Impact of Generative AI on Consumer Complaints in Financial Firms
detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is reshaping the global financial industry, yet its impact on the protection of financial consumer rights remains underexplored. With reference to contract theory, we examine the impact of financial firms’ GAI integration on consumer complaints by employing a multi-period difference-in-differences model. We utilize large language models and text analysis methods to capture GAI integration behavior among financial companies. We also deconstruct financial inclusion information based on over 16 million consumer complaint data. Our findings suggest that GAI integration lowers consumer complaints by improving financial compliance, optimizing the customer information framework. GAI integration has a more pronounced effect in reducing consumer complaints for companies providing monetary financial services and capital market services, as well as for companies with higher media exposure. From the perspective of financial inclusion, GAI integration is particularly effective in reducing complaints from consumers with low financial literacy and female consumers.

title: Do Cashless Payments Stimulate Spending? Evidence from QR Code Payment Campaigns and Bank Transaction Data in Japan
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Waseda University

detail.title: Do Cashless Payments Stimulate Spending? Evidence from QR Code Payment Campaigns and Bank Transaction Data in Japan
detail.abstract: This study examines whether cashless spending stimulates spending through subdued salience. We use bank transaction data and leverage events related to Quick Response (QR) code campaign as an instrumental variable. Our estimation offers supporting evidence for subdued salience, demonstrating that an increase in QR code payments prompted by campaigns leads to an approximately same-sized increase in other spending. However, this effect is transitory. Nevertheless, the effect of QR code campaigns on QR usage exerts a lasting impact over time, increasing the fraction of QR code users by a minimum of 1%.

title: Contracts in Crisis The War in Ukraine and Long-Term Contracts in Energy Markets
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM), Technische Universitat Berlin and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin)

detail.title: Contracts in Crisis The War in Ukraine and Long-Term Contracts in Energy Markets
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of the war in Ukraine on long-term contracts in energy markets. We find that traded contract volumes fall by 65 percent in the first months of the war. A collapse in bilateral trading contributes most to this decline. To protect themselves from price shocks, firms increasingly turned to long-term contracts already before the war. In sum, our results show that the market continued to serve firms’ hedging needs during the crisis, but bilateral trading networks collapsed, and liquidity was largely provided by centralized markets.

title: Implied Matching Functionality and Market Quality in Futures Markets
affiliations: Lakehead University, University of Manitoba - Department of Agribusiness and Agricultural Economics, University of Manitoba and University of Manitoba

detail.title: Implied Matching Functionality and Market Quality in Futures Markets
detail.abstract: This study examines the contribution of implied functionality to market quality in futures markets. During the study period, the implied functionality reduced the bid-ask spread by 0.3, 14.8, 3.5, 0.7, and 0.3 percent, added an average 59, 35, 38, 3, and 8 percent to the depth within three ticks of the bid-ask spread midpoint, and reduced volatility by 0.10, 0.74, 0.43, 0.06, and 0.03 percent in corn, lean hog, crude oil, 5-year T-Note, and gold markets, respectively. Moreover, it improved resiliency by up to 66 percent. The contribution of implied orders to all measures increased during large market movements.

title: Spatio-temporal impacts of the US Southeastern wood pellet industry on forest condition: evidence from Georgia using vegetation indices
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tulane University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spatio-temporal impacts of the US Southeastern wood pellet industry on forest condition: evidence from Georgia using vegetation indices
detail.abstract: The wood pellet industry in the US Southeast has expanded rapidly in response to growing demand from the European Union. This expansion has reportedly had no discernible impacts on forest carbon stocks, yet assessments of impacts on broader forest conditions are lacking. Here, we assess the impacts of the wood pellet industry on forest condition in Georgia over the 2004--2024 period. We test whether forest inventory plots within pellet mill procurement areas (treated) differ in vegetation indices - employed as indicators of forest condition - from those outside (untreated). Spatio-temporal variation in the inclusion was captured by three treatment variables: (1) inverse distance to the nearest wood pellet mill (proximity), (2) number of years a plot was within a procurement area (duration), and (3) their interaction. Spatial Durbin models were estimated to account for spatial dependence in vegetation indices and selected covariates across plots. Our findings point to evidence of mixed impacts. Treated plots consistently have higher vegetation indices than untreated plots, although the differences are mostly very small. However, the negative interaction between proximity and duration suggests potential long-term effects in areas under intensive and sustained procurement. Continuous monitoring and forest management practices to reduce procurement pressures seem warranted.

title: Multipollutant Cap-and-Trade Systems with Heterogeneous Firms An Optimal Transport Approach
affiliations: University of Prince Edward Island

detail.title: Multipollutant Cap-and-Trade Systems with Heterogeneous Firms An Optimal Transport Approach
detail.abstract: The simultaneous exposure to multiple air pollutants has become a pressing concern for policymakers seeking integrated market-based instruments. This paper develops and analyzes a multipollutant cap-and-trade system encompassing a diverse array of polluting firms and an independent control authority responsible for issuing multipollutant permits. Each permit bundles distinct rights to different pollutants. The authority is assumed to know the aggregate heterogeneity distribution of firms, accommodating cases where it lacks granular data on individual profiles. The central challenge lies in allocating the bundle of permits efficiently across heterogeneous firms. To address this, I leverage optimal mass transportation techniques to demonstrate the existence of an optimal allocation strategy. The allocation process is decentralized: equilibrium permit prices emerge and enable a geometric characterization of firms based on their self-selection of permits. The interaction between firm distributions, permit bundles, and payoff heterogeneity reveals strategic permit choices and market segmentation within the system. I also examine whether separated single-pollutant markets can replicate multipollutant outcomes. Numerical simulations using computational geometry and optimal transport illustrate the determination of permit prices and the induced demand partition, highlighting the feasibility and policy relevance of integrated multipollutant trading.

title: How Does Tightening Patent Protection Policy Affect Welfare?
affiliations: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research and Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research

detail.title: How Does Tightening Patent Protection Policy Affect Welfare?
detail.abstract: This study shows how households' saving responses to interest rates under the general intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) affect the welfare implications of patent protection policy. Savings act as a key channel linking patent protection to welfare through their role in financing research and development.  However, previous studies have largely neglected this dimension of welfare analysis within the overlapping generations (OLG) framework. Using an OLG framework with the variety expansion of differentiated investment goods, we show that  regardless of IES, the relationship between patent protection policy and welfare is non-monotonic and it is positive (negative) at low (complete) patent breadth. However, the stringency of the welfare-maximizing patent protection policy depends on IES, requiring a less  (more) stringent policy when IES<1 (IES>1), relative to IES=1. We then conduct empirical analysis using a cross-country panel of 48 countries from 1998 to 2017, confirming the theoretical non-monotonic relationship between patent protection policy and welfare. Our findings suggest that, governments should favor incomplete patent protection, adjusting its stringency according to households’ intertemporal substitution behavior.

title: The Determinants of Fed Policy: The Great Recession vs the Great Inflation
affiliations: California State University, Fullerton - Mihaylo College of Business & Economics and Sogang University

detail.title: The Determinants of Fed Policy: The Great Recession vs the Great Inflation
detail.abstract: We analyze the determinants of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decisions since the 1960s justified by potentially evolving beliefs—through a real-time learning process—about the structure of the economy and Markov-switching shifts in policymakers’ preferences between dove and hawk regimes. We argue that although central bank learning played an important role in the determination of Fed policy there were several shifts in policymakers’ preferences in the post-war period. We find a dovish kind of monetary policy regime present in the 1970s and early 2000s, and before the onset of the Great Recession.

title: Population Ageing and the Productivity of Public Capital: ,A Panel Cointegration Analysis of Japanese Prefectural Data
affiliations: Kwansei Gakuin University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Population Ageing and the Productivity of Public Capital: ,A Panel Cointegration Analysis of Japanese Prefectural Data
detail.abstract: This study investigates how population ageing affects the productivity of public capital, using panel data from Japan’s 47 prefectures over the period 1980–2019. We estimate a Cobb-Douglas production function and find that the output elasticity of public capital declines substantially in more aged regions, suggesting that demographic shifts may undermine the effectiveness of infrastructure investment. To improve the reliability of our estimates, we apply panel cointegration techniques that account for non-stationarity and cross-sectional dependence—a methodological challenge that has been largely underexplored in prior studies, and to which this paper makes a novel contribution. The results reveal two mechanisms: in transportation, lower land costs in ageing areas lead to overinvestment with diminishing returns; in education, dispersed facilities and youth outmigration reduce scale economies and investment efficiency. These findings imply that public investment strategies should be adjusted in line with demographic realities. Consolidation of infrastructure and educational resource integration may help sustain the productivity of public capital in ageing societies.
